findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. That covers "what is it" and "why does it matter" quickly.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: Someone visiting the Athena site sees a title about another project, firstmate. Only the third lede paragraph makes clear that most of the page is a sample study and not documentation for Athena, so the reader may not know which project the page is about.

The first section after the header is an error message. It also drops the proof the lede promises: which models did the work, the verdict, and the cost. A newcomer gets a broken-looking page and no evidence for Athena's main claims.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: This link sits in the header and is aimed at the project owner. To a newcomer it means nothing and pulls attention away from the next-step link.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: What to do next is clear and concrete. The header links to it, it lists prerequisites, and it gives one install command and one try-it command, with a note that the command acts on the current repository. It does not say whether a model account, an API key or money is needed, even though the lede stresses cost.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section (prerequisites, "./setup.sh", "athena ask \"add a changelog\"")

findings.text: The Start here section defines seven jargon terms before it says what firstmate is. Some definitions admit they are incomplete ("this page gives no test for it"), so the opening is dense for someone who only wants the gist.
findings.source: Start here → "Words used first" (captain, yolo, in scope, green, red, local-only landing, home)

findings.text: The page is honest about gaps, but several glossary entries say the term is undefined. The newcomer is left with words they cannot fully understand.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a captain call." / "...does not define a durable record." / "...does not define an endpoint."

findings.text: Bracketed claim ids link each statement to source lines at a pinned commit. That shows the traceability Athena advertises, and a reader can check it, which helps them see why Athena matters.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end."

findings.text: Hiding Counters and Transitions behind an expert toggle keeps the default path shorter for a newcomer. Even so, the core track is long and repeats itself, for example the yolo/red rule appears in Start here, the definitions list, the glossary and the claims.
findings.source: Learning path: "Show expert detail (core track is the default)"
